prompt: How do the bonding π molecular orbitals of a conjugated polyene differ from its antibonding π MOs?

choices.text: Bonding MOs have fewer nodes and lie lower in energy than isolated p orbitals
Bonding MOs have more nodes and lie lower in energy than isolated p orbitals
choices.why: More nodes means higher energy. The MOs with more nodes are the antibonding ones.

choices.text: Bonding MOs lie higher in energy than isolated p orbitals
choices.why: Bonding MOs are lower in energy than isolated p orbitals; antibonding MOs are higher.

choices.text: Bonding and antibonding MOs have the same number of nodes and differ only in how many electrons they hold
choices.why: The energy of a π MO depends on its number of nodes between nuclei, so the two kinds differ in node count.

explanation: The p orbitals of a conjugated polyene combine into π MOs whose energies depend on how many nodes they have between nuclei. MOs with fewer nodes are lower in energy than isolated p orbitals (bonding); MOs with more nodes are higher in energy (antibonding).

prompt: How many π molecular orbitals does 1,3,5-hexatriene have?
explanation: 1,3,5-Hexatriene has three double bonds and six π MOs, ψ1 through ψ6* (Figure 30.1.2): three bonding and three antibonding.

prompt: How many π molecular orbitals are filled in ground-state 1,3,5-hexatriene?
explanation: In the ground state only the three bonding orbitals, ψ1, ψ2 and ψ3, are filled. Six π electrons, two per orbital, fill three MOs.

prompt: In ground-state 1,3,5-hexatriene, which orbitals are the HOMO and the LUMO?

choices.text: HOMO ψ3, LUMO ψ4*
HOMO ψ4*, LUMO ψ5*
choices.why: Those are the frontier orbitals of excited-state hexatriene, after an electron has been promoted into ψ4*.

choices.text: HOMO ψ1, LUMO ψ6*
choices.why: ψ1 is the lowest filled orbital and ψ6* the highest empty one. The frontier orbitals are the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied.

choices.text: HOMO ψ2, LUMO ψ3
choices.why: ψ3 is filled in the ground state, so it is occupied, not the LUMO.

explanation: In the ground state ψ1, ψ2 and ψ3 are filled. The highest occupied MO (HOMO) is ψ3 and the lowest unoccupied MO (LUMO) is ψ4*.

prompt: Ultraviolet light promotes one electron of 1,3,5-hexatriene from ψ3 to ψ4*. Which orbital is the HOMO of this excited state?

choices.text: ψ3
choices.why: ψ3 still holds one electron, but ψ4* now holds one too and is higher in energy, so ψ4* is the highest occupied orbital.
ψ5* is empty in the excited state; it is the excited-state LUMO.

choices.text: ψ1
choices.why: ψ1 is the lowest-energy filled orbital, not the highest.

explanation: On irradiation an electron moves from ψ3 to ψ4*, so ψ3 and ψ4* are each half-filled. In excited-state 1,3,5-hexatriene, ψ4* is the HOMO and ψ5* is the LUMO.

prompt: 1,3-Butadiene has four π MOs (two bonding and two antibonding), and the number of nodes between nuclei goes 0, 1, 2, 3 from ψ1 up to ψ4*. How many nodes between nuclei does the ground-state HOMO of 1,3-butadiene have?
explanation: Butadiene's four π electrons fill the two bonding MOs, ψ1 and ψ2, so the HOMO is ψ2. As Section 14.1 showed, ψ2 has one node between nuclei.

prompt: According to the Woodward–Hoffmann rules, when is a pericyclic reaction symmetry-allowed?

choices.text: When the symmetries of the reactant MOs match, or correlate with, the symmetries of the product MOs
When the reactant has an even number of π electrons
choices.why: Being allowed depends on whether reactant and product orbital symmetries correlate, not simply on the electron count.

choices.text: Whenever the reaction is carried out with ultraviolet light
choices.why: Light changes which orbitals are occupied, but a reaction is allowed only when reactant and product orbital symmetries correlate.

choices.text: When the reaction passes through a stable carbocation intermediate
choices.why: Symmetry-allowed pericyclic reactions are concerted; the rule is about matching orbital symmetries, not intermediates.

explanation: Woodward and Hoffmann's rules say a pericyclic reaction can take place only if the symmetries of the reactant MOs are the same as those of the product MOs: the lobes must have the correct algebraic sign for bonding in the transition state. If they correlate, the reaction is symmetry-allowed.

prompt: What does Section 30.1 say about symmetry-disallowed reactions?

choices.text: They can't occur by concerted paths; they go by nonconcerted, higher-energy pathways or not at all
They often occur under milder conditions than symmetry-allowed reactions
choices.why: It's the symmetry-allowed reactions that often occur under relatively mild conditions.

choices.text: They occur by concerted paths, but only at very low temperature
choices.why: Symmetry-disallowed reactions can't occur by concerted paths at all.

choices.text: They give the same products as allowed reactions through the same transition state, just more slowly
choices.why: A disallowed reaction can't use the concerted path; if it happens at all it takes a different, nonconcerted, higher-energy route.

explanation: Symmetry-allowed reactions often occur under relatively mild conditions. Symmetry-disallowed reactions can't occur by concerted paths: they either take place by nonconcerted, higher-energy pathways, or they don't take place at all.

prompt: In Fukui's simplified version of the Woodward–Hoffmann rules, which molecular orbitals need to be considered?

choices.text: Only the two frontier orbitals, the HOMO and the LUMO
All of the reactant and product molecular orbitals
choices.why: That full analysis is what the original Woodward–Hoffmann rules require. Fukui's version simplifies it to two orbitals.

choices.text: Only the lowest-energy bonding orbital, ψ1
choices.why: ψ1 is not a frontier orbital unless it happens to be the HOMO; the frontier orbitals are the HOMO and LUMO.

choices.text: Only the antibonding orbitals
choices.why: The HOMO is usually a bonding orbital in the ground state; Fukui's method uses the HOMO and the LUMO.

explanation: Kenichi Fukui introduced a simplified version in which only two MOs, the frontier orbitals, need to be considered: the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO).

prompt: Who shared the Nobel Prize for the orbital-symmetry work on pericyclic reactions described in Section 30.1?

choices.text: Roald Hoffmann and Kenichi Fukui
R. B. Woodward and Roald Hoffmann
choices.why: Woodward would have shared it, but he died before the award was made.

choices.text: R. B. Woodward and Kenichi Fukui
choices.why: Woodward died before the award was made; the prize went to Hoffmann and Fukui.

choices.text: R. B. Woodward, Roald Hoffmann and Kenichi Fukui
choices.why: Woodward died before the award; it would have been his second Nobel Prize.

explanation: Hoffmann and Fukui shared a Nobel Prize for this work. Woodward would have joined them, for his second Nobel Prize, had he not passed away before the award was made.
